newsitem.title: USA: Hashimoto, Clinton to discuss trade issues Friday.
newsitem.headline: Hashimoto, Clinton to discuss trade issues Friday.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto meet on Friday amid growing fears in Washington that the trade deficit with Japan will rise sharply and spark new political and commercial tensions.

Trade is not expected to dominate Friday's session between the two leaders. They will look at all aspects of the bilateral relationship, centering on security and regional political issues. But U.S. officials said the economic relationship and specific trade items will be on the agenda.

The U.S. trade deficit with Japan fell by 19 percent last year to nearly $48 billion, its lowest level since 1991. But the gap is expected to widen again due largely to a weak yen that makes Japanese products cheaper and a strong dollar that makes U.S.-made goods more expensive.

White House officials confirmed that Clinton sent Hashimoto a letter outlining outstanding issues between the two countries but would not confirm Japanese media reports that Clinton expressed concern about the Japanese economy and the rising U.S. trade deficit.
"As we often do, we put some ideas in play that both sides can think about in advance of an important bilateral meeting," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said.
Sandra Kristoff, director of Asian affairs at the National Security Council, told reporters that the trade deficit with Japan as well as with China "is something we are looking at very closely."
The deficit with China hit nearly $34 billion last year and accounts for the second largest U.S. trade gap next to Japan.

"Surging surpluses with the United States could have a backlash here, unleashing protectionist pressures," Kristoff added. She expressed concern that a rising trade gap with Japan, after some 20 trade agreements between the two countries since Clinton took office in 1993, will make it more difficult for the administration to win new trade negotiation authority from Congress.

The administration has been without so-called fast track authority since 1994 and is seeking from Congress new legislation that will allow U.S. trade officials to negotiate trade agreements without fear they will be later changed by lawmakers. Congress may vote yes or no on an agreement, but not amend it.
Clinton is expected to raise concerns about those trade issues and about Japan's overall economy during what officials said would be about a 2-1/2 hour meeting on Friday.
The United States wants Japan to carry out further deregulation of its business sectors in the hopes that will help spur demand for U.S. and other foreign-made goods.

Kristoff said the president is likely to also discuss concerns about Japan's banking system and some specific trade issues including automobiles, shipping yards, telecommunications and airline service.

A report released last week by the U.S. Trade Representative's office and the Commerce Department said that despite progress last year in increasing U.S. car sales to Japan, progress on deregulation of car parts and on the number of dealers selling U.S. cars fell short of expectations.

The United States also seeks to resolve a longstanding dispute about Japan's shipyard practices. After several days of talks earlier this month, the United States agreed to withdraw sanctions against Japanese ships visiting U.S. ports. Japan agreed to approve some applications by U.S. carriers for port operations and promised to complete deregulation of licensing of port transportation services and reform its stevedoring services.

The United States and Japan have been negotiating a new agreement on civil aviation services. But Tokyo has been resisting U.S. calls for an "open skies" agreement that would do away with many limits on air service.
